title: Cindy Holscher wins in Kansas, holding governor's office for Democrats
description: State Sen. Cindy Holscher has won the ra
body:
State Sen. Cindy Holscher has won the race for Kansas governor, keeping the office for Democrats in a state that leans Republican. Here she's seen speaking to reporters after casting her ballot during early voting at a polling location in Kansas City, Kansas.
                
                    Jim Vondruska/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jim Vondruska/Getty Images
    

   
   Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher will hold onto the Kansas governor's office for her party after defeating Republican Ty Masterson, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Masterson, the president of the state Senate, was endorsed by President Trump. Of the 36 elections for governor across the country, Kansas was seen as the most likely to flip from Democratic to Republican control.   The race call came after days of counting the provisional ballots and with local officials doing recounts in the closely contested election.   
    Loading... 
   Current Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited after serving for eight years in a state with a heavily Republican legislature and that usually votes for Republicans for other offices and in presidential elections.   Holscher, 57, ran a campaign with notes of populism, promising to fight "sweetheart deals" for billionaires. She tied Masterson to his work in the state Senate when it passed a tax cut under former Republican Gov. Sam Brownback that led to a series of budget crises and was later repealed.   Holscher opposed school vouchers, calling for more support for public schools, in contrast with Masterson, who backed school vouchers. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and for legalizing cannabis as a way to generate state revenue.   Masterson, 57, called for lower property taxes and said faith influenced all his decisions, including in politics. He promised to be the "most pro-ag, pro-business, pro-oil and gas governor," the state has seen. He called Holscher, "the most radical, liberal, socialist Democrat ever" on a ticket in Kansas.   "He likes to throw around a whole lot of labels," Holscher responded. "You know why? Because that's all he's got."

title: Witnesses describe the D.C. shooting that left 1 dead, 4 injured
description: Local and federal law enforcement respon
body:
Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting on Thursday in Washington.
                
                    Tom Brenner/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/AP
    

   
   Busy morning crowds in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle ran for cover Thursday after a gunman opened fire at a local gym, VIDA Fitness, killing at least one person and injuring at least four others.    The gunman left the gym area, entered a nearby apartment building where he barricaded himself. Jeffery W. Carroll, the interim Police Chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, who briefed the public this morning, said at the time of the briefing that the shooter had shot himself.   A police spokeswoman later confirmed to NPR that the gunman died.   The gunman shot and killed one person inside the gym and injured another in the lobby or alley area of the building, Carroll said. The other three victims were shot across the street at a construction site, he said. One person remains in critical condition.    
   Carroll identified the gunman as a white male who had a conflict with the homeowners association of the apartment building.   The Logan Circle neighborhood sits about one mile north of the White House. The block where the shooting occurred, along 15th Street Northwest, is lined with apartment buildings, a church, coffee shops and restaurants.   
   Residents around the area described a massive law enforcement presence, including FBI agents and SWAT teams, swarming the area minutes after gunshots rang out. Residents were sent emergency text messages ordering them to remain sheltered in place. That order was lifted at around 11:30 a.m.   The first call for help came in at 8 a.m. from people inside the gym, Carroll said. Officers and other emergency responders were on scene within 30 seconds, he said. Responders found one adult man who was shot inside the gym.   Witnesses on scene told NPR that VIDA requires visitors to tap in to gain access to the fitness area. Carroll told media he believes the gunman was a member.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson//AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson//AP
    

   
   Tinbete Ermyas, an editor at NPR, was working out at the gym when the shooting started. He and other gym-goers became aware something was wrong when they heard "a very loud bang," Ermyas said.   
   "People kind of looked around at each other ... wondering what it was. Some people thought that maybe it was some weights that had been dropped. But it just sounded way too loud," he said. "The bang sort of shook everybody."   Shortly after the bang, came the screams.   "That's when we realized that it was a shooting," he said. He and others ran off the gym floor through an emergency exit that led them to a laundry room. That's where for about 20 minutes, he and others hid until police came to escort them out.   
   As they exited, they saw the body of the man who was shot.   "It was just laying there, just very bloodied and terrible. A guy that goes to the gym regularly. I see him every morning, just lying in a pool of blood. It was terrible," Ermyas said.   After the gunman barricaded himself in the apartment building, police tried for about an hour to get him to surrender safely. But Carroll said that while officers were engaging with the suspect, they heard a gunshot.   It's unclear if the gunman and the victims knew each other. Carroll said more investigation is needed.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Scorched bricks are seen, up and center right, following reports of an active shooting in Washington.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   'They were so shocked and afraid'   Next to the gym at Call Your Mother Deli, Oscar Vazquez, the manager, said he heard the fire alarm going off next door in the apartment building. Carroll, the police chief, said police believe a fire was set off in the building and the the sprinklers did go off. The fire has since been contained and put out, Carroll said.     He and his co-worker Cesar Miranda, a 22-year-old worker at the deli, said they thought it was a regular fire alarm until "we heard like 7 or 8 gunshots," Miranda said.   Vazquez said people started running out of the building said he tried to get as many people as possible into the deli.   
   "We're really worried about the people that live in the building," Vazquez said. He said they have a lot of friends and customers that live there. He said: "It was really scary. It really happened out of nowhere, just hordes of people just running down from that block."   Miranda said law enforcement were on the scene quickly.   "We saw so many people running from the area, like so many people," Miranda continued. "There was so shocked and afraid. They even started falling into the chairs that we had in the patio."

title: Colom wins Mississippi Senate race. And, White House warns Dems over future probes
description:
Colom Wins Mississippi, Trump Warns Incoming Democrats, Russia-Ukraine Talks
    
            
                
                Transcri
body:
Colom Wins Mississippi, Trump Warns Incoming Democrats, Russia-Ukraine Talks
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-153171/nx-s1-mx-6038323-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Democrat Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate seat from Mississippi, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just a few thousand votes. Colom will be the first Black Senator from the state in nearly 150 years. His win expands the Democratic majority in the new Congress to 55 seats. The Alaska race is still undecided.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Scott Colom speaks with attendees at an event held at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson, Miss. on Aug. 1, 2026.
                
                    Sarah Warnock/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sarah Warnock/AP
    

   
   🎧 Colom's win highlights growing voter concerns about affordability and the impact of the war in Iran, Elise Catrion Gregg of the Gulf States Newsroom and Mississippi Public Broadcasting tells Up First. During her campaign, Hyde-Smith relied on her record and President Trump's support, which Gregg says is no longer a winning strategy. This race signals a potential national shift, showing that the South is becoming a viable target for Democrats, Gregg says.➡️ A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year weakened the Voting Rights Act, raising the possibility of a record drop in Black Congressional representation. The Democratic blue wave lessened the expected decline, but an NPR analysis shows that Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decrease with the incoming Congress.   
   The White House is warning Democrats that their planned investigations into administration officials could cross the line into "blatant criminality." White House Counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee next year, that the administration is monitoring "abusive and capricious threats" from Democrats. The letter concludes by saying that "the administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process, motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government." Garcia said Democrats will not be deterred by threats from the Department of Justice or Trump's lawyers.   🎧 The administration's arguments may buy time and push Democrats to go to court to enforce their subpoenas, NPR's Tamara Keith says. She adds that the White House letter gives a preview of the legal arguments the administration might use next year. But more importantly, Keith says that it signals that the White House and Justice Department won't accept congressional investigations and oversight without a fight.   Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a significant prisoner swap after two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are now in Moscow today to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and attempt to make more headway to end the war in Ukraine.   
   🎧 NPR's Charles Maynes says that, going into the talks in Abu Dhabi, U.S. officials were exploring Article 5-like guarantees for Ukraine, similar to NATO's collective security defense. A move like this would be significant if implemented, but Moscow has already rejected the concept of a "NATO lite" status for Ukraine and its full NATO membership. Kushner said that, in Moscow, he aims to brief Putin directly and persuade him to involve Europeans in discussions about European security. European leaders, concerned about potential deals made without their input, are expected to join Kushner and Witkoff after these talks, when they'll meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland.   Watch this   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Abdul El-Sayed sits down for an NPR Newsmakers interview.
                
                    Bronson Arcuri/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Bronson Arcuri/NPR
    

   
   Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.   Abdul El-Sayed has made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. The 42-year-old progressive from Michigan is already calling for a new direction for his party and urging President Trump to collaborate on actionable solutions. El-Sayed said that voters have temporarily entrusted Democrats with power, but warns that they risk losing that trust if they don't act boldly. As the senator-elect comes into the new role, he is advocating for new Democratic leadership in Congress, an end to the war in Iran, the passage of "Medicare for All" and the abolishment of ICE. While he acknowledges the challenge Senate Democrats face with a majority that's a few seats shy of being filibuster-proof, he remains open to working with his new Republican colleagues. In conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, El-Sayed reflects on the recent elections, the future of the Democratic Party and the need for impactful legislation in the upcoming years.   
   Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.   Deep dive   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Ford Motor vehicles are displayed for sale at the Leif Johnson Ford dealership on June 30 in Austin, Texas.
                
                    Brandon Bell/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Brandon Bell/Getty Images
    

   
   The average price for a new vehicle in the U.S. has hit a record high of $51,109, according to Kelley Blue Book. This figure is about $500 above the previous record set in December 2025. For years, car prices have remained high, primarily due to supply chain issues stemming from the pandemic. But there's some good news: While that new high sets a record, it only represents a 2.1% increase over the past year. This means the price is rising more slowly. If you're in the market for a car, here's what to know:   🚗 Used cars are also more expensive. The average used car now costs close to $27,00, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive.🚗 New vehicles cost more partly because it takes more money for automakers to make them. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and imported goods from Canada affect American automakers, who assemble the vehicles on both sides of the border. Computer chips used in sensors and electronics also cost more, thanks to competing demand from data centers.🚗 Americans tend to prefer larger vehicles, such as SUVs and trucks, which often come with a higher price tag, according to Kelley Blue Book.🚗 Drivers today tend not to want entry-level cars. Instead, they are increasingly drawn to more expensive features, like 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                U.S. actor Stacy Keach poses on May 15, 2018, during a photocall for the film "Gotti" at the 71st edition of the Cannes Film Festival in Cannes, southern France.
                
                    Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Actor Stacy Keach has died at the age of 85 after a long battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure. His diverse roles included policemen, cowboys and Shakespearean characters.In this week's Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Ricci Shryock sends greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers practice for their country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games.Russia's top independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, is shutting down after more than 30 years due to Kremlin pressure from the Ukraine war and censorship laws.   
   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
description: President Trump signed the final steel b
body:
President Trump signed the final steel beam at the White House ballroom the day after the midterm elections.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.   He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."   That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.   
   His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.   Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction, packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court.   Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.   
   Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."   When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Jared Huffman, center, poses with activists protesting Trump's triumphal arch at Memorial Circle in May. He will soon become the chair of the committee with legislative and oversight authority over public lands.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Imags
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Imags
    

   
   Rep. Jared Huffman, D.-Calif., told NPR in an interview that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says a Democrat-led Congress will fight back.   
   "There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," said Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks.   
   Huffman says blocking Trump's construction projects — and holding people accountable for potential wrongdoing — will be a top priority when he leads the committee. Earlier this week, he sent letters ordering dozens of administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation.   "Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said.   What would that actually look like? Democrats have many tools at their disposal, from legislation to lawsuits. But experts say only two are likely to succeed: funding and oversight.   Democrats could block funding for specific projects, potentially as soon as next month   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump made a final pre-Midterm Day pitch to voters from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, whose renovations took months longer than anticipated due to algae blooms and peeling paint.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Congress could — at least in theory — pass laws to block specific projects from moving ahead. Some Democratic lawmakers have already introduced bills to protect the Kennedy Center from demolition and prohibit the construction of an arch at Memorial Circle.   But Trump has promised to "veto everything," and Democrats won't have a big enough majority to override him on their own.   "Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds."   The Constitution says that the federal government may spend money only if is appropriated by Congress. But Trump has neither sought nor received congressional authorization for projects like the arch and the White House ballroom — he maintains he doesn't need it.   
   Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is one of many who disagree. She's the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department.   "Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage."   Pingree says a Democratic majority will be able to write appropriations bills with clear language from the outset about where money can and can't be spent — and potentially take the president to court if he doesn't follow it.   Super expects Congress would prevail in such a challenge, because it has clear-cut authority over federal funds.   
   For example, he noted that some of Trump's D.C.-area beautification projects have been funded at least in part by diverted national park entrance fees. Congress could "cap how much money can be used in the greater Washington area, and force the money to be used in the Everglades and Yosemite and Great Smoky Mountains," he said.   Congress will have to make some appropriations decisions in the coming weeks, since it needs to pass a short-term funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown. Democrats could use that opportunity to try to limit funding for at least one of Trump's construction projects.   Huffman has proposed language that would prevent Trump from using federal funds for the East Potomac golf course renovations, limiting them instead to repairs of the park's crumbling seawall. Pingree said she will join him in fighting to negotiate that into next month's bill.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                On one October Saturday, the Trump administration cut down some 430 trees at East Potomac Park, where the president wants to develop a municipal golf course into a championship-level course.
                
                    Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
    

   
   "Whether or not the president will sign that with that in there, I don't know yet," she said. "But certainly those are the most … immediate crisis points … People want the president to stop cutting down the trees on the golf course and stop trying to take that over, and they want to make sure that no shovel goes into the ground on building the arch."   
   Earlier this year Pingree introduced an amendment that would have outright blocked construction of the arch; it failed along party lines. She wonders whether any Republicans might vote differently after the midterms, given the message Americans sent at the polls.   "They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. "And if every time the president gives a speech, he's either standing in front of the Reflecting Pool, which he spent millions of dollars on, or showing you the new marble choices he's putting into the ballroom, it just makes a lot of people mad."   Pingree said she's been surprised to hear how strongly people feel about these projects – even people well outside D.C. And she agrees with them that potential corruption and misuse of taxpayer dollars are worth fighting: "After the first of the year, we will use every tool in our toolbox."   Democrats want to hold people and companies accountable    Lawmakers and experts acknowledge that not every project is reversible, or potentially even worth the fight. Huffman suggested he will focus on bigger projects, and ones that are moving too fast for courts to adequately rein in.   "Are we going to throw all of our efforts at stopping the gilding of every statue in Washington, D.C.? Probably not," said Huffman. "But these are iconic places that we're talking about, with permanent damage that we need to engage on to try to prevent."   
   Even so, Democrats could decide that certain construction projects are "the price they pay for other priorities," said Claire Leavitt, a professor of government at Smith College. Voters made clear they want lawmakers to focus on ending the Iran war and making life more affordable, big asks that may take a lot of political capital.   "And that's not corruption or Democrats not doing their job," Leavitt said. "It's just the natural trade-offs of dealing with who you're dealing with, and understanding that what matters to Trump more than anything seems to be building the arch, building the ballroom … remaking the Kennedy Center."   
   Whether or not these projects move forward, Congress can provide a fuller public accounting of how they came to be — in the hopes of preventing more in the future.   "They can gavel in hearings. They have agenda-setting power," Leavitt said. "They determine what the public hearing roster is. They decide which witnesses to invite. And that means they have a unique opportunity to draw negative public attention to the Trump administration."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Work on the White House ballroom is moving quickly.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   That may be easier said than done, especially with an administration that has pointedly refused to comply with congressional oversight and is now warning Democrats that their future investigations could constitute criminality. Huffman was coy when asked how he is preparing to handle such challenges.   "We are going to have to have a strategy and a plan to do these things that prior Congresses have never imagined they would have to do," he said.   One investigative priority, lawmakers say, will be following the money — especially when it comes to donations for the ballroom and other projects. Leavitt says that focus has an added benefit: Private companies and individuals are likely more willing to testify than a member of the administration.   Another example: Congress could subpoena for information about the decision-making processes of the Kennedy Center board and the physical state of the building, which trustees say must be closed for two years of repairs. And it can put that information in the Congressional — and therefore historical — Record.   "Both the current public can make its judgments, and history can make its judgments," Leavitt said.   
   Leavitt said oversight can often lead to policy change in the longer term. For example: The committee investigating the Jan. 6 insurrection didn't stop Trump from eventually pardoning Capitol rioters, but it did lead Congress to pass an electoral reform act.   "The frustrating part about congressional oversight is Congress can draw attention to a problem, and they can demand accountability for something that's already been done," Leavitt said. "But it's very hard for Congress to stop something from happening that the president is determined to do."   
   Super agrees that Democrats are playing a long game. He expects to see more bipartisan support after Trump leaves office for preventing future presidents from following his playbook.   "The process in the past has been built on trust, and President Trump certainly broke that trust in numerous ways," he said. "Laws can be written so that we don't depend on trust, we depend on law. And I'm guessing we're going to do that."

title: At least 23 states considered laws governing ICE and schools this year
description:
Hokyoung Kim for NPR
    

   
   Catch up on what you mi
body:
Hokyoung Kim for NPR
    

   
   Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.      Andrea Garza says it's not unusual or alarming when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are spotted near a school in Laredo, Texas, a border town.   In other parts of the country, "seeing the presence of border patrol would be, you know, different, maybe shocking. Just something from another world, right?" she said. "It's something very normal here."   Garza is a school leader with the United Independent School District, which serves Laredo. Federal data shows 94% of her district's community is Hispanic. Garza said some families have been in Laredo for generations, while others came more recently, and the federal government is one of her area's largest employers.   
   She said she knows what she would do if ICE comes knocking: If they don't have a warrant or subpoena, they don't get in.   "We serve 'in loco parentis' for students," she said, meaning "in place of a parent" when the students' rights are challenged.   "It's not interpreted, in the way we see it, as interfering with the law," Garza explained. "It is more just verifying that we are all following the law."   Texas state law prohibits local entities, including campus police, from obstructing federal immigration enforcement. But NPR found no state laws that directly address how much access these officers should have in K-12 public schools.   
   And it's not just Texas. Many states lack clear policies governing what these interactions should look like. Recent federal changes haven't helped.   At the beginning of President Trump's second term, the administration rescinded a policy that protected schools, among other "sensitive" places, from immigration enforcement.   "Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America's schools and churches to avoid arrest," a statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said at the time. "The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense."   
   In some places, school leaders and researchers say Trump's immigration policies have led to enrollment drops.   DHS, which houses ICE, has said that ICE does not raid or target schools.   But reporting from K-12 Dive shows the last academic year still saw several incidents of ICE agents on school grounds. When that happens, education leaders often rely on a patchwork of state and district policies to know what to do.   This year, many state legislatures tried to update those policies.    Loading... 
   An NPR analysis found that, so far this year, at least 23 states have considered new legislative proposals — in some cases multiple proposals — governing federal immigration officers and K-12 public schools.   The vast majority of the state proposals NPR reviewed — 35 out of 40 — sought to limit federal officers' access to K-12 campuses and students; only one proposal — in Mississippi — sought to ensure that schools cooperate with ICE. The rest didn't explicitly limit or increase access or cooperation.   Thomas Saenz is president and general counsel of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, an organization that advocates for Latinos living in the U.S. He said the elimination of the federal sensitive locations policy is likely driving many states to establish their own protections, "belts and suspenders, as they say."   But while lawmakers seem to agree there's a need for clearer policies, in many places, they've struggled to find consensus over what those policies should be. Of the 40 proposals NPR reviewed, only 12 had become laws as of early this school year.   From requiring a warrant to requiring cooperation   Minnesota, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Maine and Nebraska are among the state legislatures that considered restricting ICE access to schools.   Several of these proposals specified the need for a warrant. Others aimed to restrict what school police and school resource officers, or SROs, can and can't do, including when it comes to immigration-related arrests.    
   On the other side of the spectrum, Mississippi considered and passed a law requiring government entities, including school districts, to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.   And a few states considered requiring school boards to adopt policies outlining how they would respond to immigration authorities on school property.   At least eight states already had laws governing immigration enforcement and K-12 schools at the start of 2026. A few of those states — including Connecticut, Maryland and Oregon — considered additional legislation this year.   
   Recent state proposals have also aimed to allow public schools to charge tuition for students who aren't U.S. citizens or legal immigrants. Such proposals would challenge the decades-old landmark Supreme Court ruling Plyler v. Doe, which established that all children, regardless of immigration status, have the right to a free K-12 public education.   NPR did not include these proposals in its analysis. According to reporting from Education Week, as of July, at least two states were considering proposals challenging Plyler. Similar efforts failed in at least five other states.   Proposals target sensitive locations and student enrollment   Following the Trump administration's decision to rescind the policy protecting "sensitive" places, some states have been trying to set their own rules around where immigration enforcement can and can't go.   
   A few states — including West Virginia, Hawaii and Kansas — made a push this year to restrict ICE access by designating school campuses as sensitive locations. None of those three states' proposals passed.   Some states already have laws that explicitly ban or restrict these types of sanctuary policies. That didn't stop Missouri from considering a proposal this spring to limit school cooperation with immigration enforcement. An existing state law prohibiting municipalities from adopting sanctuary policies and requiring cooperation calls into question how far such a proposal could go.   Lawmakers in Tennessee considered multiple proposals this year from across the political spectrum, including one to track K-12 students' legal status, which opponents argued was part of an effort to challenge Plyler, and another that would require schools to immediately notify all students, parents and employees if immigration officers were on school grounds.   
   "As legislators, we cannot make informed decisions without data, and right now we simply do not know what the attendance is in our school systems across the state, regarding children who are here illegally," Tennessee Rep. Jason Zachary (R-Knoxville) said in a March hearing, where he spoke in favor of the measure that would have required schools to report students who are undocumented.   The bill did not make it to a final vote.   Meanwhile, another Tennessee proposal this year would have prohibited certain sensitive areas, including schools, from being used as staging areas, processing locations or operational bases for immigration enforcement.   "Everybody deserves to have a great learning environment, and it's hard to teach when you are worried that one of your students is going to be taken," Tennessee Rep. Gabby Salinas (D-Memphis), who sponsored that bill, told NPR. The proposal ultimately failed.   Minnesota principals await legislation   NPR was not able to find a pre-existing state law in Minnesota. But after the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year, lawmakers considered at least five different proposals around ICE and schools.   They ranged from stricter warrant requirements to mandating that schools develop procedures for handling requests from law enforcement. None of the five proposals made it to a final vote.   That means school leaders like Principal Kenny Newby are left waiting.   Newby leads Justice Alan Page Elementary School in Maplewood, Minn., just outside the Twin Cities. He said if ICE ever comes to his school, his goal is to be kind, stay calm and be firm.   In the absence of state laws, he said he has his own district's policies to lean on: Staff members are supposed to welcome the ICE officers, start a conversation, ask for required paperwork and notify school-level administrators. Those administrators then reach out to district leaders.   
   If the officers have a warrant, they would be directed to the district office for next steps. Newby stressed: "We would not allow them to have direct contact with students."   Rob Reetz is the principal of Mounds View High School in nearby Arden Hills. He said it would be helpful to have a state law governing how schools are supposed to interact with federal immigration officers; if nothing else, a law like that could simplify interactions between districts.   Right now, Reetz said, if a sports team from his school travels to play against a team from another district and ICE shows up at the game, it's unclear which district's protocols adults should follow.   Still, if ICE does come knocking at his school, Reetz worries they won't necessarily follow rules set by the state or any other entity.   He said he remembers learning in January that federal agents had been spotted at Roosevelt High School in Minneapolis. At the time, MPR News reported that armed U.S. Border Patrol officers came onto school property during dismissal and "began tackling people, handcuffed two staff members and released chemical weapons on bystanders."   "It contributed to this uncertainty about how would our interactions go with immigration enforcement if they were to be on our campus," Reetz said.   Newby echoed these concerns. He said he and his staff would feel more supported if there were "clear expectations on keeping schools a safe place."   Edited by: Nicole CohenAudio produced by: Lauren MigakiResearch by: Natalie Pate, Nicole Cohen, Sarah Knight and Barclay Walsh

title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from DA to Mississippi's Democratic U.S. senator
description: Democrat Scott Colom gives an update on
body:
Democrat Scott Colom gives an update on the Senate race against Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith on Nov. 4 in Jackson, Mississippi.
                
                    Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images
    

   
   JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.   But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.   "We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend — we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."   
   Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.   Flipping red counties with a focus on affordability    Colom won by approximately 5,000 votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.   While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58% of the vote.   Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County — an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base.   Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.   "I believed that the majority of the Mississippians love our state more than they hate the Democratic Party or love the Republican Party," Colom said. "They want their kids to have good schools. ... They want to be able to make sure that young people, if they want to stay in Mississippi, can have a job. They want the hospitals to stay open."   
   While Colom isn't surprised that his message resonated this year with voters, he faced obstacles when a federal judicial nomination stalled in the U.S. Senate in 2023, when then-President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship.   Mississippi's Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican, indicated he would support his nomination.   
   The state's junior senator, Hyde-Smith, blocked him. She cited donations from billionaire philanthropist George Soros around Colom's run for DA, which in 2023 Colom said were to an independent PAC — not his campaign.   She also said he opposed legislation to protect female athletes in a statement provided to the Mississippi Free Press at the time.   In a letter to Hyde-Smith, Colom said he didn't know what she was referring to and noted that he'd signed a statement saying he wouldn't use law enforcement resources to criminalize doctors who offer gender affirming care to transgender youth.   He also stated in the letter that if he was confirmed as a judge, any of his personal views would be irrelevant to his "daily work." And he asked the senator to reconsider — she didn't.   Three years later, she was defending her seat from him. She was confident on election night that she'd beat him, telling her supporters, "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator."   
   She instead lost and on Wednesday night, she issued a statement conceding the race, saying she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.   A narrow victory that "made a difference"   Colom recognized that attention from national Democratic leaders, and his party's campaign funds, came late this year, but he noted that it was the attention his campaign received from voters within the state that made the difference.   "They understand the power of their vote in ways that we really haven't seen in a long period of time, because if you look at these margins, certainly everything that everybody did made a difference," Colom told reporters in Jackson just days before the election was called.   
   Being elected as a Democrat is no small feat either. The last time Mississippi sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982 and an incumbent hasn't been defeated since 1942.   Colom now also holds the distinction of being the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction.    It's something he's proud of — but not the laurels he's resting on.   "My job is to be a senator that makes it easier for the next African American that has the work ethic, the vision, the values, and they want to be United States senator, make it easier for them," Colom said. "I am a person that is continuing to show up in the community and take the tough questions and explain my, you know, live my values. And if I do that, it makes it easier for the next person to be judged by their character and not their skin color."   While his victory is historic, his campaign has also made waves — especially on social media. In an interview with WLOX, Hyde-Smith responded to questions about beef affordability by suggesting folks pick a different protein.   Colom hit back, with a campaign ad, suggesting folks pick another senator instead.   Eventually, the rest of the country started listening. About two weeks before the election, the PAC associated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer donated $1.2 million for advertising.   
   And several big-name Democrats also ended up joining Colom on the campaign trail: former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former President Bill Clinton and U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, to name a few.   Colom traveled the whole state — from the coast to the capital, up to the Tennessee border. While in the Mississippi Delta, he said what he wants to do while in the Senate all goes back to his home of Columbus.   "I've always been committed to trying to make my community better, trying to make my city better, trying to make my state better, and that's what running for United States Senate is all about for me," Colom said. "It's a continuation of a service that runs in my family and I was raised [by] my community and my church to give back and that's why I'm doing it in this moment."   
   Tiara Jackson of Mississippi Public Broadcasting contributed to this report.

title: Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
description: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., seen above
body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., seen above on Aug. 8, 2026 in St. Paul, Minn., has announced he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate Majority Leader.
                
                    Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
    

   
   Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate majority leader, pushing the party into a fresh debate over its future just days after sweeping victories in the midterm elections.    Van Hollen made the announcement on Thursday, saying voters sent a clear message in the midterms — that they want "change from the status quo."    "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said in a statement. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."   
   Van Hollen, 67, was elected to the Senate in 2016 after spending more than a decade in the House representing a Maryland suburb outside of Washington, D.C. One of his party's more progressive members, he gained national attention last year lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after he was wrongfully deported to a prison in El Salvador.    His announcement comes at a moment when progressive activists, as well as some Democratic lawmakers, are calling for Schumer, 75, to be replaced as party leader. Schumer has served in the role since 2017, but drew the ire of many inside the Democratic base for not taking a tougher stance against President Trump during a fight over government funding in early 2025.    "I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer wrote on social media following Van Hollen's announcement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters at the Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   While Schumer has maintained he has the votes to become majority leader, he has faced growing resistance from inside the Democratic caucus. Earlier this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont Independent who aligns with Democrats, said he would oppose Schumer. He made the announcement next to Michigan Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who did not say outright she would oppose Schumer, but told reporters, "I am seeking change."    
   Several incoming Democratic lawmakers have similarly expressed opposition to Schumer's bid for majority leader, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed.    
   "I deeply appreciate Senator Schumer," El-Sayed told NPR this week. "But this is about leadership for the American public, and if all we do is kind of go back to what we've been doing in a moment where we've been given a mandate, I worry that we may not earn our mandate."   Multiple Democrats have publicly come out in support of Schumer, including Arizona's Ruben Gallego, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks.    Democrats will vote by secret ballot for majority leader in early December. Whoever wins will preside over a majority of 55 seats, though that could grow to 56 depending on the final tally in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.

title: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say
description: Paper copies of amendment votes are set
body:
Paper copies of amendment votes are set on display near the Senate Chamber, on July 1, 2025 on Capitol Hill.
                
                    Tom Brenner For The Washington Post via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner For The Washington Post via Getty Images
    

   
   If you want to know what bills are under consideration in the Senate, you could follow floor proceedings live on C-SPAN. But, even for parliamentary procedure experts, it can be difficult to understand exactly what's happening.   Among the issues? The text of what the lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. Now, a crosspartisan group of open governance advocates has sent a letter to Senate leadership calling for change. In the letter, first obtained by NPR, they call on the Senate to post bill and amendment text online as soon as it is made available to members.   
   "The public and the press and the whole apparatus that supports the Senate to help understand what legislation is, they don't have access," said Daniel Schuman, an author on the letter and the executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to strengthening the institutions of American democracy.   
   That lack of transparency means "that problems can often sneak through," said Schuman. "At times, this has been a mechanism for the Senate to move legislation to avoid the proper public scrutiny." In 2013, Schuman recalled, Congress quietly repealed provisions of a popular congressional financial disclosure and insider trading law — skirting public scrutiny.   While the Congressional Record — the official record of legislative branch proceedings and debates — does provide information about bill text and proposed amendments, it is not published until after the legislative day concludes. That means when bills or amendments are offered on the same day they are considered, they may not be publicly available until after they are voted on.   "We've been working first to get the Senate to update their own systems internally," said Luke Hogg, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, which works to help policymakers become more effective stewards of innovation.    The organization joined AGI on the letter, and as Hogg explained, now that staffers themselves have reliable access to what is being considered, "it should also be given to the American public."   
   In contrast to the Senate, the House of Representatives publishes draft legislative text and proposed amendments online ahead of their consideration, with rare exceptions.   
   The letter argues that the current Senate process creates unequal access to information, where staff and interest groups with connections to Senate offices understand what's being considered, but legislative support agencies like the Congressional Research Service and the Government Accountability Office, as well as the press and public at large are often left in the dark.   "Privileged access to public business that currently is the subject of floor debate should be minimized to the extent possible," the letter says.   The advocates hope to see the Senate enact the public transparency effort in the new Congress in January.    In a statement to NPR, an aide to Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Democrat who is expected to become chairman of the Senate Rules committee, said that the senator is open to input on the transparency measure as well as other ideas to improve the functioning of Congress.   Sen. John Thune, Senate Republican leader, did not respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say

title: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
body:
Democratic Reps. Terri Sewell (left) and Shomari Figures of Alabama appear at a voting rights rally in May on the steps of the state's Capitol in Montgomery, Ala.
                
                    Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
    

   
   A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that further weakened the Voting Rights Act raised the possibility of a record drop in Black representation in Congress.   But a Democratic blue wave in the midterm elections helped forestall such a decline for now.   Most notably, Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, won reelection despite Alabama's Republican state leaders making his district far more GOP-leaning after the court's decision.   
   Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decline next year, according to an NPR analysis based on race calls by the Associated Press as of Thursday afternoon. The incoming Congress is set to include at least 60 Black House members, including nonvoting members, down from 63 in the current House. That's just one away from the record loss of four Black representatives after the 1876 election, around the end of the Reconstruction era.   In addition to the unprecedented mid-decade redistricting fight, the usual churn of politics, including members retiring or running for higher office, contributed to next year's falling tally.   
   But high Black voter turnout, especially in the South, fueled Democratic wins that have offset the upcoming decline in the number of Black members of the House.   Voting rights advocates and redistricting experts warn, however, that the redrawing of district lines in the coming years, including after the 2030 census, continues to pose a threat to Black representation in Congress.   A "Black wave" helped Black Democrats overcome redistricting hurdles in the South   Heading into this year's midterms, Figures faced tough odds of keeping his House seat in Alabama, where voting has been racially polarized between a Republican-supporting white majority and a Democratic-supporting Black minority.   
   Figures joined Congress after the 2024 election as the first Black representative of the state's 2nd Congressional District. As part of a long redistricting battle, a lower federal court had ordered the district to be drawn to include a Black population large enough to have a realistic opportunity of electing their preferred candidate.   For the midterms, though, the Supreme Court's conservative majority allowed Alabama's Republican-controlled legislature to redraw the district. That ruling came weeks after the high court released its landmark decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened the Voting Rights Act's protections against racial discrimination in political mapmaking.   
   The new lines of Alabama's 2nd District, the lower court had previously found, were "tainted by intentional race-based discrimination" and would "afford Black-preferred candidates zero chance of winning there." Based on the redrawn map, Figures appeared to be on track to leave Congress like Rep. Cleo Fields, the Louisiana Democrat who decided not to seek reelection after the Supreme Court's Callais ruling struck down the Black opportunity district Fields represents.   "It took a remarkable level of turnout in order for [Figures] to be able to win," says Cliff Albright, co-founder and executive director of Black Voters Matter. "Some are calling it a blue wave. For us, particularly here in the South, we're calling it a Black wave because what we saw was the Black electorate's been motivated by the attacks on our voting rights, by the gerrymandering that was taking place."   
   New voting maps in Texas and Florida led to the undoing of some Black-represented districts, but Democrats' sweeping victories in other states are helping to counteract those losses.   North Carolina's GOP-controlled legislature redrew the district of Rep. Don Davis, one of the state's three Black representatives, but Davis defended his seat. And two incoming Black House Democrats — Cyril Jefferson and LaKesha Womack — flipped districts long represented by white Republicans.   Democratic socialist Reps.-elect Melat Kiros in Colorado and Donavan McKinney in Michigan are also adding to the tally.   And Democrats are set to take control of statewide offices and legislative chambers in Texas and other places that were long-standing Republican strongholds.   By breaking the GOP trifecta in Georgia, for instance, the blue wave lowered the redistricting threat facing the state's congressional districts represented by Black Democrats. Last week, Georgia's outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced he will not call a special session on redistricting before handing the office in January to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will be the country's first Black woman elected governor.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Don Davis, a Democrat from North Carolina, speaks at a 2024 campaign event for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in Greenville, N.C.
                
                    David Yeazell/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        David Yeazell/AP
    

   
   Upcoming redistricting could result in fewer Black representatives   But Albright, of Black Voters Matter, sees this year's midterms as unique.   
   "What happens two years from now or four years from now, where it's not the same wave year, where there's not the same economic realities across the country, where you don't necessarily get the same number of white voters that decide, 'Oh, I guess I can vote for this Democrat'?" Albright says. "It's simply not sustainable for Black voters to be carved up and have our voting power that diluted and for it to not have an impact over a more sustained period of time."   And while midterm successes are leading some Democratic politicians to declare a generational shift in U.S. politics, Kareem Crayton, a redistricting expert and vice president of the Brennan Center for Justice's Washington, D.C., office, is taking a more wait-and-see approach.   "This sounds a lot like what people said in 2009 after a lot of massive change happened, including in the South, with the election of Barack Obama. And it wasn't two years later that people sat in a haze, looking at returns that pretty much wiped out many of those changes that favored Democrats, including Black Democrats," Crayton says. "It could be that this is a start of a generational shift, but it might not be. And if you're thinking about how rules ought to be crafted, I think the cautious approach is always the preferable approach in making certain that rights under the worst conditions are protected as opposed to the most rosy scenarios."   
   Crayton says current redistricting rules, shaped by the Supreme Court's decisions in Callais and other cases, set up the potential dismantling of more opportunity districts for Black and other racial minority voters in future years. This past year's redistricting rush was limited partly because the Callais ruling came too late for many states to redraw their maps in time for the midterms.   "I think people who are looking at the recent Supreme Court decision around Callais and how it would be implemented always understood that the greatest reaction to that would not be in 2026, but would be 2028, 2030 and onward," says Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies, which tracks Black representation in Congress.   
   And that reaction is likely to reach beyond Congress, adds Janai Nelson, president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund, which represents a group of Black Louisiana voters in the Callais case.   "When we look at state legislatures, when we look at city councils, when we look at school board maps and we look at any other elected office that relies on districts, those have largely been untouched by Callais up until now," Nelson says. "But as we enter a new state legislative process where these maps may be redrawn, then we might see devastating impact in electability by Black voters across the country and especially in the South."   There's no redistricting, however, for U.S. senators. And on that side of Capitol Hill, Black representation is on the rise. The blue wave of the midterms has lifted the number of Black senators in the new Congress to a historic high of seven. They include Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and fellow Democrat Scott Colom, who is set to become the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

schema.headline: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
